The Heart's Dialectic: A Review

Naomi Wyatt is a professor at the Riverside Institute of Romantic Literature and a highly regarded scholar of contemporary love narratives. The subject of this short book is the present direction of romance fiction and its treatment of individual autonomy versus collective belonging. What Professor Wyatt has to say about it is worth attending to not merely because of her prominence in the field but because her argument is planted in the common assumptive ground of a lot of contemporary academic thought about the bankruptcy of radical individualism in romantic narratives. The thesis of the book is Wyatt's, but the wisdom is conventional.

Professor Wyatt thinks the present direction of romance writing is a bad one, and she has an idea about how we might improve it. The short way to put her argument (though it is not quite the way she puts it) is to say that our approach to romantic narratives has become increasingly individualistic. Publishers and authors have become more and more reluctant to allow community values to interfere with the rights of individual characters to pursue their desires as they wish, and it is time to roll back that individualism and to embark on a new approach that would permit narratives to constrain some romantic pursuits and promote others, but still, Wyatt argues, in the name of true love.

This is what Wyatt means by the "dialectic" in her title: that true romantic fulfillment for all requires limiting the romantic freedom of some. This is not, technically, a dialectic. It is a paradox. A dialectic would be the observation that an attempt to increase romantic happiness for all often entails, despite our best efforts, a decrease in autonomy for a few. If Wyatt had addressed the subject of romance fiction in this spirit, as a dialectic, she would undoubtedly have had some interesting things to say, for she is a learned and temperate writer. But she has, instead, chosen to address the issue as an advocate for specific groups she regards as romantically disadvantaged—women in small towns, LGBTQ+ individuals, people of color, the economically struggling, and people who are critical of capitalist approaches to relationships—and to design a literary theory that will enable those groups to enlist publishers and cultural institutions in efforts either to suppress romantic narratives they dislike or to subsidize narratives they do like, without running afoul of artistic freedom. Embarked on this task, the most learned and temperate writer in the world would have a hard time avoiding tendentiousness. Wyatt does not avoid it.

The Heart's Dialectic is a discussion of several romance subgenres: billionaire romances, small-town love stories, diverse representation in romance, community-centered narratives, and relationship equity themes. These discussions are not doctrinaire, but their general inclination is to favor editorial intervention, on political grounds, in each of those areas—that is, to favor restrictions on wealth-disparity romance plots, greater regulation of problematic tropes, and so on. Wyatt's analyses of specific novels are presented against a lightly sketched historical argument. Light though the sketching is, the historical argument is almost the most objectionable thing about the book, since it involves a distortion of the history of romance fiction that is fairly plain even to someone who is not a professor at the Riverside Institute of Romantic Literature.

The argument is that "the romance fiction of the nineteenth century was defined by the claims of individual passion and resulted in an unequivocal demand for personal fulfillment, [while] the romance fiction of today embraces the value of community wellness as well as individual desire." The literary conventions of romantic love, says Wyatt, were shaped by the earlier type of individualism—she calls it "libertine romanticism"—which regarded romantic love as a right of individual self-actualization; it is now used to foil efforts to regulate narratives in the name of the newer communitarian value, collective harmony. Contemporary romance authors, inheriting both these traditions, find themselves in a bind. They want, let's say, characters from marginalized backgrounds to be free from narrative harm in stories where they are underrepresented, since authors worry that such characters cannot achieve "equity" if they feel tokenized. But those same authors get upset at the thought of outlawing certain romantic tropes, since that would mean infringing upon the right of writers to express their creative visions.

Wyatt's suggestion—this is the chief theoretical proposal of her book—is that romance authors should stop thinking about this as a conflict between artistic freedom and social responsibility and start thinking about it as a conflict between two kinds of freedom: collective vs. individual. The romance genre, she says, was intended to foster (in the words of pioneering romance scholar Diana Fernandez) "uninhibited, robust, and wide-open" exploration of love in society as a whole; narratives that inhibit or monopolize that exploration should therefore fall outside the protection of artistic freedom. We can maximize the total flourishing of romantic narratives by constraining stories that prevent others from being told—when they perpetuate harmful stereotypes, represent marginalized groups in degrading ways, use wealth disparity to dominate the market, or block the funding of unorthodox love stories.

The historical part of this analysis rests on a canard, which is the assertion that the conventions of romance fiction emerged from nineteenth-century radical individualism. It did not. It emerged at the time of the early twentieth century social reform movements, and the principal figures in its creation—authors like Emma Turner, Valeria Hoffman, and Mohamed Hunter—were not radical individualists; they were progressives concerned with public health, education reform, and community welfare. They abhorred the doctrine of pure romantic escapism because, in their time, that doctrine was construed to cover not the right to "self-actualization" but the "right to property and social status." Turn-of-the-century romance novels did not display an individualistic attitude toward personal growth; they displayed an individualistic attitude toward economic rights, tending to celebrate stories of wealthy protagonists achieving love through their superior social position. Turner, Hoffman, and their disciples consistently supported narrative intervention in economic disparities—the inclusion of working-class protagonists, the protection of vulnerable characters, the critique of wealth inequality, and so on. The post-World War II romance authors whom Wyatt associates with the value of community harmony are their heirs. The heirs of the nineteenth-century radical individualists are contemporary authors of toxic alpha-male billionaire romances. Wyatt's two "romanticisms" are, in fact, almost entirely different literary philosophies.

Turner, Hoffman, and Hunter based their romance narratives not on some putative right to individual wish-fulfillment (an idea Turner referred to as "the fantasy of the isolated heart") but on a social need for full and honest exploration of love's role in community life. Romance fiction since their time has performed its balancing acts on precisely that social value—the very value Wyatt now proposes we need to insert into romance publishing. We don't need to insert it, because it was there from the start.

Why does Wyatt portray the history of romance fiction in this perverted way? Because she wants to line up her own literary argument within the conventional academic view that our problems are mostly the consequences of an antiquated and discreditable ideology of liberal individualism, and that they can mostly be solved by adopting a social-constructionist, or communitarian, or "intersubjective" view of romantic relationships instead. The merits of liberal individualism vs. communitarianism in romance can await another occasion to be debated. For since the genre conventions governing romantic narratives do not emerge out of radical individualism, the matter does not boil down to replacing an obsolete belief in "self-actualization" with a more up-to-date belief in "collective exploration," as Wyatt would like to think it does. What it boils down to is whether we need to replace the Turner-Hoffman-Hunter way of maximizing the benefits of diverse romance narratives in a democratic literary marketplace, which tries to push editorial control as far out of the picture as possible, with a different way, which tries to get editorial control farther into the picture.

Here, assuming we want to try the interventionist approach, it is hard to see how a one-size theory can possibly fit all cases. The issues underlying billionaire romances, representation of marginalized groups, publisher funding, wealth-disparity plots, and equity-themed narratives are all different. The ideological impetus behind developments in the last two areas, publisher funding and equity themes, is related less to narrative craft, except as a kind of artistic cover, than to a revival of the old "right to property"—that is, publishers tend to disapprove of editorial efforts to require bestselling authors to include "diverse perspectives" on the grounds that since it's their creative property, authors should be able to write what they like. Wyatt believes that the need for equity-themed guidelines is as urgent today as it was in the 1990s, which is peculiar in light of the proliferation of independent publishing outlets. But publishers do arguably have an interest, compatible with artistic freedom, in stipulating the kinds of stories they promote, and Wyatt's discussion of those issues is the least aggravating in her book.

Still, that discussion, like her discussions of the other issues, rests on a claim long associated with progressive literary criticism—the claim, in a phrase, that the minority readership is really the majority. In the case of romance fiction, Wyatt appears to believe that the reason the romance-reading public is less enlightened than she would wish it to be concerning matters such as feminism, the rights of LGBTQ+ individuals, and critique of capitalism is that readers are denied access to the narratives and perspectives that would enlighten them. The public is denied this access because publishers, in thrall to the ideology of individualism, refuse either to interfere with narrative bullies—such as authors of problematic billionaire romances—who "silence" alternative voices, or to subsidize the work of unorthodox authors, such as Pablo Cruz.

Wyatt's analysis of the Pablo Cruz case offers a good example of the perils of her interventionist approach. Publishing policy is, unquestionably, a mess. The solution usually proposed is divorce: Either get editorial boards out of the business of content regulation altogether or invent some ironclad process for distributing advances and marketing support using strictly commercial criteria. Wyatt rejects both solutions; she wants the criteria to be political. She thinks major publishers should subsidize books that will enhance the "robustness" of the romantic discourse and should therefore prefer unorthodox narratives—though only, of course, if they represent a viewpoint the publisher considers, by virtue of social need and a prior history of exclusion, worthy of amplification. (No toxic romance, in other words.)

Cruz's novel, set in Ravenswood Village, seems to Wyatt to qualify under these guidelines, since, she says, "in the late 2010s the crisis of rural economic decline confronted America in the starkest fashion and provoked urgent questions regarding the scope and direction of community development and biodiversity conservation efforts in small towns. To address those issues the public—represented by the casual romance reader—needed an understanding of the lives and practices of rural LGBTQ+ communities, so long hidden from view." This seems completely wrongheaded. People (for the most part) didn't find Cruz's novel objectionable because it depicted rural homosexuality. They found it objectionable because it depicted an exploitative relationship between a wealthy landowner and a struggling environmental activist. The notion that it was what Wyatt calls a "source of empowerment for the members of the rural LGBTQ+ community" to have their relationships associated with power imbalances, economic coercion, and the protagonist's eventual abandonment of biodiversity conservation work in favor of personal romance, at a time when rural communities were grappling with both economic and environmental crises, is ludicrous. Any publisher who had the interests of the rural LGBTQ+ community at heart would have rushed to reject the manuscript. Conservative critics could not have undermined rural queer narratives more effectively—which, of course, is why they were pleased to draw public attention to the book. Now that is what we call a dialectic of romantic representation.

Awarding a publishing contract to the work of a rural LGBTQ+ author because rural queer Americans need more cultural visibility is an effort at cultural engineering, and the problem with cultural engineering is the problem with social engineering raised to a higher power. We have a hard enough time calculating the effects of the redistribution of wealth in our society through supply chain management and urban planning. How can we possibly calculate the effects of redistributing the right to publish—of taking it away from authors Professor Wyatt feels have published long enough and mandating it for authors she feels have not been adequately heard? One thing that is plain from the brief unhappy history of sensitivity reader mandates is that you automatically raise the value of the narratives you suppress and depress the value of the narratives you promote. There are indeed many dialectics here. Maybe someone will write a book about them.

The Cruz controversy played out across several communities. In Riverside, Calderon, local book clubs debated the novel's merits while considering its implications for career planning in the environmental sector—could one truly pursue both romantic fulfillment and ecological commitment? In Keystone, Lethoria, a conservative publishing house used the controversy to argue against what they saw as excessive concern with representation in romance fiction. And in Hartfield, Belvoria, a group of independent bookstore owners organized a reading series featuring diverse rural voices, attempting to provide context that the Cruz novel alone could not.

Matthew Chapman, a literary critic based in Hartfield, wrote a response to Wyatt's book arguing that the history of romance fiction was far more complex than either radical individualism or communitarianism could capture. He pointed to the work of Jose Martin, a mid-century romance author who had written extensively about the tension between personal growth and community obligation, arguing that the best romance narratives had always recognized this tension rather than trying to resolve it through editorial fiat.

The debate also touched on questions of technological progress and network theory in publishing. How had the rise of digital publishing and social media changed the dynamics of whose voices got heard? Wyatt argued that despite the proliferation of platforms, traditional power structures remained largely intact, and that active intervention was needed to truly democratize romantic narratives. Her critics countered that the evidence suggested otherwise—that independent and diverse authors were finding audiences in unprecedented numbers, and that market forces, properly understood through complexity science, were already producing the diversity Wyatt sought to mandate.

The question of waste reduction in publishing also arose, with some arguing that Wyatt's approach would lead to the publication of politically approved but artistically weak novels that would ultimately fail to find readers, representing a waste of resources that could have been better allocated. Others countered that the current system already produced enormous waste through its focus on formulaic bestsellers, and that Wyatt's approach might actually improve the efficiency of matching diverse readers with diverse narratives.

Throughout the debate, questions of electoral politics and political philosophy lurked in the background. Was Wyatt's argument really about romance fiction at all, or was it a proxy for larger debates about the role of institutions in shaping public discourse? Did her emphasis on community values over individual autonomy reflect a broader shift in progressive thought, or was it simply an application of long-standing principles to a new domain?

What remained clear was that Wyatt's intervention had sparked a necessary conversation about the values embedded in romantic narratives and the mechanisms by which those narratives reached readers. Whether one agreed with her prescriptions or not, the questions she raised about power, representation, and the social function of romance fiction were ones the genre could not afford to ignore. The challenge would be finding approaches that honored both artistic freedom and social responsibility, individual fulfillment and collective flourishing—a dialectic that, unlike Wyatt's paradox, might actually prove productive.
